extracted.intended_audience: general literate readers of The Spectator / educated 18th-century periodical audience
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and moralizing essays in the style of The Spectator (early 18th‑century periodical), addressing human character, benevolence, love, trees, eternity, and theatrical observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity before judging others
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you can be qualified to see and animadvert on the Failings of others, you must be pure your self.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by a vision in which a phantom cuts open the narrator, squeezes out his heart (removing his own sinful qualities) and only then permits him to examine the hearts of acquaintances. Implies an ethical rule: cleanse or examine your own faults before criticizing others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspect inward causes, not outward appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: Many things which I had always cherished as Virtues, issued out of my Heart on this Occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The vision shows that what appears virtuous may conceal faults; evaluative attention must search inner causes (the 'fomes' or spot in the heart) rather than rely on outward reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition/resentful spleen diagnosed by heart agitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tom Dread-Nought — his heart shot up and down with incredible swiftness; the fomes was of a red fiery Colour. He rails at better Men and is for ever uneasie because his Merit is insufficiently rewarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A red, active spot (fomes) and an agitated heart indicate ambition, choler, and perpetual discontent from perceived lack of reward; useful as a diagnostic image of corrosive resentment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avarice manifests as small, black, lethargic heart
rubrics_metrics.description: Dick Gloomy — the heart was remarkable for its Smallness, lay still at the Bottom of the Phial, the Fomes was quite black and almost diffused over the whole Heart. He thirsted after Money and became melancholy and despairing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A small, darkened, slow-beating heart symbolizes greed leading to misery and isolation — a criterion for recognizing avarice by its dampening effect on life and cheer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity appears as a small conspicuous spot
rubrics_metrics.description: Will. Worthy — a large fair Heart, the Fomes or Spot was exceeding small; whatever way soever I turned the Phial it always appeared uppermost and in the strongest Point of Light. The speck discovered is Vanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small but prominent spots, visible in the brightest light, indicate vanity even in otherwise good persons; suggests evaluating the visibility and position of a fault when judging character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misinterpreting emotion for ill-will
rubrics_metrics.description: Freelove — a small swelling spot taken at first for Ill-Will was only Passion and wholly disappeared upon nearer Inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent hostile signs may be passion or temporary feelings; recommendations: inspect closely before condemning, distinguishing permanent malice from passing emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large multicolored fomes indicates coquetry
rubrics_metrics.description: A Female Heart: the Fomes in it of the largest Size, and of a hundred different Colours, which were still varying every Moment — belonged to Coquetilla.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A vividly multicolored, changing spot is read as coquetry; the passage sets a symbolic diagnostic rule for reading affective behavior by internal signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudery may appear to grow on scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Melissa, a noted Prude — the Fomes at first Sight very small, but as I looked stedfastly upon it, it grew still larger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some faults (prudery/self-righteousness) become more apparent under scrutiny; evaluators should note how a perceived trait changes with attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innocence lacks visible blemish
rubrics_metrics.description: Seraphina — enclosed a Heart in which, though examined with utmost Nicety, I could not perceive any Blemish. You are not to wonder that you see no Spot in an Heart, whose Innocence has been Proof against all the Corruptions of a depraved Age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of visible 'spot' functions as criterion for genuine innocence; if any blemish exists it may be too small for human eyes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceit represented by fomes running in twisted veins
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Hearts of other Females the Fomes ran in several Veins, which were twisted together, and made a very perplexed Figure. I was told it represented Deceit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex, vein-like spreadings of the spot signify deceit; interpreters should associate structural patterns of 'blemish' with corresponding moral vices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two principles of human action: Self-love and Benevolence
rubrics_metrics.description: Man ... hath wisely furnished it with two Principles of Action, Self-love and Benevolence; designed one of them to render Man wakeful to his own personal Interest, the other to dispose him for giving his utmost Assistance to all engaged in the same Pursuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating human motives and behaviour, treat self‑love and benevolence as distinct driving principles rather than reducing one to the other; moral evaluation should account for both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs that pity is disinterested benevolence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pity which arises on Sight of Persons in Distress ... Children and Persons most Thoughtless about their own Condition ... feel the most violent Touches of Compassion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate pity in children and thoughtless persons (who cannot anticipate reciprocal benefit) is evidence of natural, disinterested benevolence; therefore such spontaneous compassion counts as genuine benevolent motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure from relieving others indicates non‑selfish motive
rubrics_metrics.description: The Satisfaction of Mind which is the Consequence of having removed them into a happier State ... are instead of a thousand Arguments to prove such a thing as a disinterested Benevolence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The internal delight at doing good, even if pleasurable, does not prove selfishness; evaluators should distinguish pleasure-as-result from motive-as-cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical trade-off: benevolence supports self-love
rubrics_metrics.description: Benevolence, though a distinct Principle, is extreamly serviceable to Self-Love, and then doth most Service when 'tis least designed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing actions, note that benevolence may further personal interests (e.g., social reciprocity), but this instrumental effect does not negate its moral reality; look for independent benevolent disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical 'creed' on Eternity and God (four articles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles: (1) It is certain that no Being could have made it self; (2) That therefore some Being must have existed from all Eternity; (3) That whatever exists after the manner of created Beings ... could not have existed from Eternity; (4) That this eternal Being must therefore be the great Author of Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as demonstrative points for reasoning about God's existence; useful as a checklist of premises when forming philosophical arguments about eternity and a necessary being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veneration and preservation of ancient trees
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not without the utmost Indignation, that I observe several prodigal young Heirs ... felling down the most glorious Monuments of their Ancestors Industry, and ruining, in a Day, the Product of Ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive cultural standard: value and preserve ancient trees as monuments of ancestry and public good; felling them for novelty or convenience is condemned as prodigality and cultural ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ancient/traditional reasons for protecting trees (sacred status)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Heathens ... regarded it as the highest Piece of Sacrilege to injure certain Trees ... Stories of Erisicthon, the Grove of Dodona, and that at Delphi are Instances of this Kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing for conservation, appeal to historical and religious precedents that treated some trees as sacred; these authorities serve as cultural-rhetorical criteria for environmental respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casuistic rules for amorous conduct (Love Casuist cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of delicate questions to decide amorous behavior: How great the Contraction of the Fingers must be before it amounts to a Squeeze by the Hand; What is an absolute Denial from a Maid vs a Widow; What Advances a Lover may presume to make, after receiving a Patt upon his Shoulder from his Mistress's Fan; Whether a Lady at the first Interview may allow an Humble Servant to kiss her Hand; How far permitted to caress the Maid in order to succeed with the Mistress; What constructions to put upon a Smile vs a Frown; On what Occasions a sheepish Look may do Service, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposes a casuistical (case-by-case) framework for adjudicating permissible amorous signs and advances — an attempt to supply fine-grained social rules for courtship and interpreting signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxims about Love (collection)
rubrics_metrics.description: A series of aphorisms: 'There are more Calamities in the World arising from Love than from Hatred.' 'Love is the Daughter of Idleness, but the Mother of Disquietude.' 'Men of grave Natures are the most constant; ... Men should be more constant than Women.' 'The Gay Part of Mankind is most amorous, the Serious most loving.' 'A Coquet often loses her Reputation, whilst she preserves her Virtue.' 'A Prude often preserves her Reputation when she has lost her Virtue.' 'Love refines a Man's Behaviour, but makes a Woman's ridiculous.' 'Love is generally accompanied with Good-will in the Young, Interest in the Middle-aged, and a Passion too gross to Name in the Old.' 'The Endeavours to revive a decaying Passion generally extinguish the Remains of it.' 'A Woman who from being a Slattern becomes over-neat, or from being over-neat becomes a Slattern, is most certainly in Love.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A cluster of heuristics for diagnosing and characterizing love and lovers; these operate as prescriptive-observational rules for commentators and social critics when interpreting romantic behavior.
